title: Stacks & Queues
summary: Use a stack when the newest item should come out first, and a queue when the oldest item should come out first.
refresher: A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds, pop removes the newest item. A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue adds to the back, dequeue removes the oldest item from the front.

advanced-stack-lifo.title: Stack order means newest first
advanced-stack-lifo.body: A stack behaves like a pile of trays. The last item you add is the first one you remove.
advanced-stack-lifo.example: push A, push B, pop -> B
advanced-stack-lifo.notice: Do not remove from the front when the question says stack.
advanced-stack-lifo.mistake: Mixing up stack and queue order gives the right operations in the wrong order.

sections.title: Stack: newest item first
sections.summary: A stack remembers work in reverse order.

blocks.body: A stack is useful when the most recent thing matters first. Undo buttons, browser back history, and matching parentheses all use this idea.

blocks.caption: Push adds to the top. Pop removes that same top item.

python.code:
stack = []
stack.append("A")
stack.append("B")
top = stack.pop()
print(top)

blocks.title: Name the end you remove from
blocks.body: A stack removes from the same end where it adds. If you add at the back, pop from the back too.
A queue is useful when the first item waiting should be handled first. Lines at a desk, print jobs, and breadth-first search use this idea.

blocks.caption: Stack and queue differ only in which item leaves next.
blocks.wrong: Add A, add B, remove B
blocks.right: Add A, add B, remove A

blocks.prompt: You add A, then B, then C to a stack. What comes out first?
blocks.why: A stack removes the newest item first, so C comes out first.

blocks.prompt: You add A, then B, then C to a queue. What comes out first?
blocks.why: A queue removes the oldest item first, so A comes out first.
